headings.text: 🌳 Decision tree: do I need WebRTC at all?

notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection

The section answers one question: how do two endpoints you don't control exchange live media when neither can accept an unsolicited packet? The browser solves the media and the traversal. You build the signaling, the relays and the server in the middle, and you pay for whichever path the user's network forces.

Concept map

The framing note sets three phases. Signaling and SDP carry the setup, ICE and NAT behaviour decide the path, and the topology, transport and voice notes put it into a product (voice AI also builds on topologies).

Green is CORE, blue SUPPORTING, yellow BREADTH. Neighbours sit outside the map: NAT below it, choosing a transport beside it, and the voice pillar's media transport above it.

Decision tree: do I need WebRTC at all?

The default is a WebSocket, because every other leaf adds signaling, relays and a media stack you then operate.

  • LL-HLS over a CDN (what WebRTC is for): changes if the audience starts talking back.
  • WebSocket (WebSocket): changes if the payload becomes media that must be played on time.
  • PCM over WebSocket (WebRTC vs WebSocket): changes if a client joins over Wi-Fi or cellular.
  • WebRTC (ICE, STUN, TURN): changes if UDP is blocked everywhere you serve, which leaves TURN over TLS and TCP under the media anyway.

Decision tree: which topology?

The default is peer-to-peer with a TURN fallback, because it runs no media server. A server must earn its place by consuming the media or by saving clients' uplinks.

  • P2P plus TURN (topologies): changes the day you add recording, transcription or an agent.
  • SFU (topologies): changes if server egress, n(n-1) streams per room, outgrows the budget for very large rooms.
  • MCU (topologies): changes if receivers can decode several streams again; then the transcode cost isn't worth paying.

notes.title: WebRTC — Breadth Flashcards
notes.html:
Three topics that hang off what WebRTC is for and ICE, STUN, TURN.

WebRTC's transport stack

Stage: secure · per connection

Everything rides one UDP flow on the ICE-nominated pair. DTLS handshakes over it and exports the keys for SRTP (RFC 5764), so DTLS sets up keys and SRTP protects each media packet. Data channels take the other branch: SCTP inside the same DTLS association. RFC 8827 §6.5 forbids plain RTP and requires DTLS for data. SRTP encrypts the payload but leaves RTP headers (sequence number, timestamp, SSRC) readable and authenticated, so a capture still shows loss and reordering. One failed DTLS handshake kills media and data together. SDP carries the fingerprint that binds it.

Data channels

Stage: frame · per packet

A data channel carries your bytes between peers over SCTP inside the media's DTLS association (RFC 8831), so it costs no new handshake. Reliability is tunable per channel: maxRetransmits or maxPacketLifeTime, never both (the browser throws TypeError), and ordered, true by default. Zero retransmits with unordered delivery gives a UDP-like service, right for cursor positions or game state the next update replaces. It's a free side effect of a call you already have; to reach your own backend, use a WebSocket. The three APIs covers the API.

Media pipeline basics

Stage: frame · per packet

Between microphone and speaker: an encoder (Opus for audio in 2.5–60 ms frames, VP8, VP9, H.264 or AV1 for video), RTP packets, then the receiver's jitter buffer, which trades delay for smoothness and grows on a lossy path. RTCP carries the feedback: NACK asks for a retransmission, PLI asks for a fresh keyframe because later frames depend on it, and REMB or TWCC feed congestion control (GCC), which tells the encoder what bitrate the path bears. Simulcast lets an SFU pick a quality per receiver. Codecs and frames: audio for engineers.

notes.title: What WebRTC Is For — Live Media Between Endpoints That Can't Accept a Call
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 8825: WebRTC overview · 📜 RFC 8827 §6.5: communications security · W3C: WebRTC Recommendation · WebRTC for the Curious: applied WebRTC

TL;DR

WebRTC gets live audio, video and data between two endpoints that both sit behind NAT and can't accept an unsolicited packet. The browser does capture, traversal and encrypted UDP media; you build the signaling that introduces the peers and the servers that carry what traversal can't. Three phases, three failure modes: signaling breaks and nothing starts, ICE breaks and it hangs in checking, media degrades and the call sounds bad.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:① capture② offer and answer over your channel③ candidates trickle④ ICE checks nominate a pair⑤ DTLS keys SRTP⑥ media flows⑦ consent checks every ~5 s

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does the browser give you? Capture, a peer connection with NAT traversal, a data channel.
What does WebRTC not define? Signaling. You build it.
Can media be unencrypted? No. SRTP is mandatory; NULL ciphers are forbidden (RFC 8827 §6.5).
Signaling server dies mid-call. What happens to media? Nothing. Only renegotiation and new calls fail.
Who in the middle acts on a session? NATs, a TURN relay if needed, an SFU if you run one.
Draw by hand: the three phases Offer, answer and candidates via signaling; STUN checks peer to peer; DTLS, then SRTP.

The idea

You want two browsers talking. The obvious design opens a socket from one to the other, and it fails twice. Neither browser can listen for an inbound connection, and both sit behind NATs that drop any packet they didn't ask for. If you route the audio through your server over a WebSocket instead, every lost segment makes the frames behind it wait, so a two-bar phone hears a stall instead of a blip.

WebRTC fixes both inside the browser. Each side discovers addresses where it might be reachable, and both send probes at the same time, so each NAT opens a mapping for the other's packets. Media then rides UDP, where a lost packet is concealed, not waited for, and it's always encrypted.

What it doesn't do is introduce the peers. The offer, the answer and the candidate addresses must reach the other side over a channel you pick and run, and anything stateful beyond two people (rooms, recording, a relay, an agent) is a server you also run.

The trade: the hardest real-time parts come free, and you pay with a set of stateful services sized by your users' networks: signaling, STUN, TURN and usually an SFU.

How it works

One call, three phases. The numbers match the Flow line.

Signaling is two legs each way through a server you run; everything after ④ goes peer to peer, or through a relay or an SFU, never through signaling.

Rule What actually happens
Signaling Not in any spec: JSEP only says descriptions must be exchanged. If it fails, nothing starts.
Connectivity ICE pairs every candidate and probes in priority order. If no pair works, it stays in checking, then failed.
Media DTLS keys SRTP on the nominated pair. Loss degrades quality; it doesn't drop the call.
Liveness Each side refreshes consent with a STUN check every ~5 s. With no answer for 30 s it stops sending (RFC 7675).
The middle NATs decide whether a direct pair exists, TURN relays when none does, and an SFU replaces the far peer for anything past two people.

Evolution

Lineage:2002 offer/answer (RFC 3264)2010 ICE (RFC 5245)2018 ICE revised (RFC 8445)2021 WebRTC RFCs and W3C Recommendation2025 Recommendation updated
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. Every major browser ships it, the W3C Recommendation was updated on 13 March 2025, and the realtime voice APIs from model providers use it.
  • Changed in RFC 8827: encryption stopped being a configuration choice. A gateway or recorder that expects plain RTP must terminate DTLS-SRTP itself.
  • What's next and what won't change: standard HTTP signaling for one-way cases (WHIP) and IETF work on media over QUIC are pushing at the edges. The need to traverse NAT and to own the stateful services won't change.

On the wire

Illustrative browser code: the three APIs in the order you call them. signal is your own channel.

const pc = new RTCPeerConnection({
  iceServers: [
    { urls: "stun:stun.example.net:3478" },                       // reflexive candidates
    { urls: "turn:turn.example.net:3478", username: u, credential: c }, // relay fallback
  ],
});
const mic = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true }); // ① HTTPS + permission
mic.getTracks().forEach((t) => pc.addTrack(t, mic));            // before the offer: it describes them
pc.onicecandidate = (e) => e.candidate && signal.send({ candidate: e.candidate }); // ③ trickle
pc.ontrack = (e) => (speaker.srcObject = e.streams[0]);          // ⑥ remote media
pc.onconnectionstatechange = () => log(pc.connectionState);      // ICE + DTLS, the one to show users
await pc.setLocalDescription();                                  // ② creates the offer implicitly
signal.send({ description: pc.localDescription });              // WebRTC never sends this for you

Break it: does a call depend on the signaling server staying up?

# our TCP "signaling" swaps two UDP ports, then exits; peers then send 20 ms "frames" for 1 s
a, _ = sig.accept(); b, _ = sig.accept()
a.sendall(b.recv(256)); b.sendall(a.recv(256)); sig.close()   # offer/answer done, server gone
# each peer: u.sendto(b"frame", far) every 20 ms and count what arrives
socket.create_connection(SIG)   # → ConnectionRefusedError
# look for: frames still arriving at both peers after the server is gone
# naive belief predicts: zero frames, because "the call goes through the server"

Run on Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026, on 127.0.0.1. With the signaling server refusing connections, each peer received 45 frames in the second. The media path never touched it, which is why a signaling deploy should cost you new calls, not live ones.

Measure it

  • See it: chrome://webrtc-internals during a call shows the nominated candidate pair, dtlsState: connected, and bytes rising; correct is all three, with signaling idle.
  • In production: setup success per session, split by phase (signaling round trip, ICE, DTLS), plus relay share. A falling setup rate with healthy live calls points at signaling.
  • Bounded by: a peer that vanishes → consent expiry stops sending after 30 s. A setup that never completes → a client setup timeout, one ICE restart, then fail visibly.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: WebRTC is the browser's stack for live media between endpoints that can't accept inbound connections. It captures the mic, punches through NAT with ICE, and sends encrypted media over UDP with loss handling built in. It deliberately leaves signaling to you, so the first thing you build is the channel that introduces the peers. Production is rarely pure peer-to-peer: TURN and an SFU carry what traversal can't.

Q · Mechanism — What does the browser do, and what do you still build? The browser does capture behind a permission prompt, then candidate gathering, connectivity checks, the DTLS handshake, SRTP keying, congestion control and loss recovery, all inside three APIs. You build everything with state: the signaling channel, identity and room membership, short-lived TURN credentials, recording, and any server that consumes media. The split is the shape of the system. The real-time parts are solved, and the distributed-systems parts are yours.

Q · Trade-off — When is WebRTC the wrong tool? When nobody replies live, and when it isn't media. A broadcast audience needs seconds of latency, not hundreds of milliseconds, so low-latency HLS over a CDN gives caching and no per-viewer state. Messages between a client and your own backend need one WebSocket, not signaling, STUN and TURN. WebRTC earns its four services when someone answers what they hear, over a last mile that loses packets. See the tree in the chapter map.

Q · Failure — A group feature ships on the 1:1 code and calls fall apart at five people. What ran out? Client uplink and encoder CPU. In a mesh each participant encodes and sends its stream to every other participant, so the weakest uplink caps the room. It presents asymmetrically: everyone else sees one person freeze, and that person's own view looks fine. Confirm with outbound bitrate and quality-limitation reasons per sender in getStats(). The fix is topological, an SFU, as the arithmetic in topologies shows.

Q · Design — 1:1 calls, occasional 20-person rooms, and a voice agent that can join any call. Where does media go? The binding constraint is the agent: a model doesn't run in the browser, so media must reach a server in every session. That settles it: an SFU for all sessions, including 1:1. Switching from peer-to-peer at three people means two media paths, two recording stories and a transition that fires when the call matters most. Client to the nearest SFU edge, TURN beside it, the agent joining as a participant, signaling as its own service. Watch relay share first. See the WebRTC flow design.

Compare

Media path Hops Encrypted to Who carries the bytes When you'd pick it
Direct pair peer to peer the far peer nobody 1:1, no server needs the media
Relayed pair peer, TURN, peer the far peer your TURN, both directions no direct pair exists
Via an SFU peer, SFU, peers the SFU your SFU, n(n-1) streams out groups, recording, agents

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Media encryption SRTP and SRTCP, no NULL ciphers data channels must use DTLS spec: RFC 8827 §6.5
Consent check interval 5 s default, randomised 0.8–1.2× keeps a live pair proven spec: RFC 7675 §5.1
Consent expiry 30 s then the sender must stop spec: RFC 7675 §5.1
Frames delivered with signaling down 45 per peer in 1 s 20 ms frames on 127.0.0.1 measured: Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "WebRTC is peer-to-peer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the API is called RTCPeerConnection, and every tutorial connects two tabs.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: groups need an SFU, recording and agents need media on a server, and users without a direct pair go through TURN.
    ↳ Think instead: peer-to-peer capable. The far "peer" is usually your server.
  • "WebRTC is a protocol"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one name, one browser API.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's ICE, STUN, TURN, DTLS, SRTP, SCTP and RTP under one API, tied together by RFC 8825. "WebRTC isn't working" names no layer.
    ↳ Think instead: name the failed phase: signaling, ICE or media, because each has a different fix.
  • "I can read the audio with tcpdump if I need to"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: plain HTTP habits, where encryption is optional.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: SRTP is mandatory and NULL ciphers are forbidden, so a capture shows RTP headers and encrypted payload.
    ↳ Think instead: instrument from the endpoints: getStats() and the SFU's counters are your packet capture.
  • Not the same: signaling failure vs media failure
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both reach support as "calls are broken".
    ↳ Difference: signaling down stops new calls and renegotiation; media problems degrade calls already running.
    ↳ Think instead: new calls failing while live calls are fine points at signaling; the reverse points at the path.
  • Don't use WebRTC for a broadcast nobody answers.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the low-latency video stack you already know.
    ↳ What goes wrong: per-viewer connections, per-viewer bandwidth, and nothing a CDN can cache.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: low-latency HLS or DASH over a CDN, accepting a few seconds of delay.
  • Don't stand up WebRTC to send JSON to your own backend.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: data channels sound faster than a WebSocket.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you take on signaling, STUN, TURN and ICE to reach a server that has a public address anyway.
    ↳ Do instead: a WebSocket. A data channel only pays off beside media you already have.
  • Shelf life: the phases and RFC 8827's rules are durable. Signaling standards for one-way media (WHIP, WHEP) and QUIC-based media are still moving.

Connections

Path:NATwhat WebRTC is forthe three APIssignalingICE, STUN, TURN
  • Builds on when UDP is right: why live media prefers loss to waiting.
  • Owned elsewhere: topologies owns the mesh arithmetic; breadth cards own DTLS-SRTP and the media pipeline.
  • Contrasts with WebRTC vs WebSocket: when one socket to your server is enough.
  • Bounded by ICE, STUN, TURN: the relay that catches users with no direct pair.
  • Decided in the WebRTC flow design: the end-to-end system.
  • Drilled in WebRTC call setup.

notes.title: The Three WebRTC APIs — Capture, Connection, Data, and Three State Machines
notes.html:
References

W3C: WebRTC Recommendation · MDN: getUserMedia() · MDN: connectionState · MDN: RTCDataChannel

TL;DR

getUserMedia returns live tracks after a permission prompt, on HTTPS only. RTCPeerConnection is the engine: ICE, DTLS, SRTP and congestion control. RTCDataChannel rides the same DTLS association for arbitrary bytes. The connection exposes three state machines, and watching the wrong one gives you "connected, but no audio".

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:getUserMediaaddTracknegotiationneededoffer and answerICE, then DTLSconnectionState: connectedontrack on the far side

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which state should the UI show? connectionState: it aggregates the ICE and DTLS transports.
What does addTrack mid-call trigger? negotiationneeded: a fresh offer and answer through signaling.
Set both maxRetransmits and maxPacketLifeTime? TypeError. Pick one; ordered is separate.

The idea

Your call screen turns green on iceConnectionState === "connected", and support tickets say "connected, but silent". ICE found a working pair, but the DTLS handshake on it then failed, so no SRTP keys exist and no audio can flow. The other bug is the mirror image: a Wi-Fi blip moves the state to disconnected, your code hangs up, and a call that would have recovered in two seconds is gone.

The peer connection reports three subsystems separately. signalingState tracks the offer and answer, iceConnectionState tracks connectivity checks, and connectionState folds ICE and DTLS together. Each moves on its own.

The trade: one object hides ICE, DTLS and SRTP from you, and you pay by having to pick the right state machine for each decision.

How it works

The one to drive the UI from. disconnected is a pause, not an end.

new comes before connecting and closed after close(). Only failed justifies action, and the action is an ICE restart, not a new call.

Rule What actually happens
signalingState stable, two offer states, two pranswer states, closed. It returns to stable after every exchange and says nothing about packets.
iceConnectionState Connectivity only. It can read connected while DTLS is still handshaking or has failed.
connectionState ICE and DTLS together; the honest "is the call up?".
Tracks Added before the offer, because the offer describes them. Adding later means renegotiation, so turning a camera on mid-call is a round trip through signaling.
Data channel SCTP inside the existing DTLS, so no new handshake. The first channel on a connection still triggers renegotiation.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. The W3C Recommendation was updated on 13 March 2025, and all three APIs are in every major browser.
  • Changed in the current API: setLocalDescription() with no argument creates the offer or answer itself, so negotiation code no longer branches on caller and callee.
  • What's next and what won't change: additions arrive as extensions (encoded transforms, stats). The split into capture, connection and data, and the three states, are settled.

On the wire

Illustrative handlers: decide on connectionState, debug with the ICE state, and make a channel that never retransmits.

pc.onconnectionstatechange = () => {
  if (pc.connectionState === "connected") showLive();
  if (pc.connectionState === "disconnected") showReconnecting();  // wait: it often recovers
  if (pc.connectionState === "failed") pc.restartIce();           // new ufrag/pwd, same call
};
pc.oniceconnectionstatechange = () => log("ice", pc.iceConnectionState); // diagnosis only
const cursor = pc.createDataChannel("cursor", {
  ordered: false,       // a late position is useless
  maxRetransmits: 0,    // send once; never with maxPacketLifeTime (TypeError)
});

Measure it

  • See it: chrome://webrtc-internals lists all three states with timestamps; correct is connected on both ICE and the peer connection, plus a DTLS transport in connected.
  • In production: per session, time in disconnected and the share that recover without a restart; failed count and ICE restarts. A rising failed share on one network points at its NAT or firewall.
  • Bounded by: a transient blip → wait out disconnected before acting. A dead path → restartIce(), then fail visibly instead of hanging.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Three objects cover the browser side. getUserMedia returns tracks after a permission prompt on a secure page. RTCPeerConnection gathers candidates, negotiates, runs DTLS, keys SRTP and carries tracks with congestion control. RTCDataChannel rides the same DTLS association with reliability you can turn down. The trap is the three state machines: show users connectionState, debug with the ICE state, and don't hang up on disconnected.

Q · Mechanism — Why can ICE say connected while the call has no audio? Because ICE and DTLS are separate steps. ICE proves a path; DTLS then runs over it to agree keys for SRTP. A fingerprint mismatch or a blocked handshake fails DTLS with ICE still connected. connectionState aggregates both transports, so it reads failed where the ICE state looks healthy. That's why it drives the UI.

Q · Trade-off — When does a data channel beat the WebSocket you already have? When the peer connection already exists and the traffic is between peers and time-sensitive: cursor positions, game state, control messages. It reuses the DTLS association, skips the server hop, and can drop late messages. A WebSocket wins for anything bound for your server, anything the server must see, and anything needed before the call exists, signaling included. The data channels card has the reliability modes.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
connectionState values 6 new, connecting, connected, disconnected, failed, closed spec: W3C WebRTC
iceConnectionState values 7 adds checking and completed spec: W3C WebRTC
Reliability knobs on one channel at most 1 both set throws TypeError spec: W3C WebRTC

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: connectionState vs iceConnectionState
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both have a connected value and fire on the same events.
    ↳ Difference: the ICE state covers connectivity checks only; connectionState also includes DTLS.
    ↳ Think instead: users see connectionState; engineers read the ICE state to learn which half broke.
  • Don't hang up on disconnected.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the word sounds final.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a brief lapse in checks, such as a Wi-Fi roam, becomes a dropped call.
    ↳ Do instead: show "reconnecting", wait, and call restartIce() only on failed.
  • "addTrack mid-call just starts sending"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's a method call on a live connection.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the new track isn't in the session until a fresh offer and answer complete.
    ↳ Think instead: adding media is renegotiation, which is why glare handling matters.
  • "A data channel has its own setup cost"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it looks like a separate connection.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's SCTP inside the DTLS association the media already uses, on the same ICE pair.
    ↳ Think instead: free beside media, expensive alone, because alone it needs signaling, ICE and TURN.
  • Don't call getUserMedia at page load.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it gets the permission prompt out of the way.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a prompt with no context gets blocked, and undoing a block means a trip to site settings.
    ↳ Do instead: ask when the user chooses to join, and warm up the peer connection meanwhile.
  • Shelf life: the three APIs and states are settled. Stats fields and extensions keep growing.

Connections

Path:what WebRTC is forthe three APIssignalingSDP
  • Builds on what WebRTC is for: the three phases these objects carry out.
  • Owned elsewhere: browser capture owns capture constraints and device handling.
  • Used by signaling: negotiationneeded and glare live there.
  • Contrasts with WebSocket: the channel for anything bound for your server.

notes.title: Signaling — The Channel WebRTC Leaves to You
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9429 §3.1: JSEP signaling model · 📜 RFC 8838: Trickle ICE · 📜 RFC 9725: WHIP · MDN: perfect negotiation

TL;DR

Signaling carries an offer, an answer and a trickle of candidates between peers that can't reach each other yet. JSEP leaves the transport, addressing, retransmission, forking and glare to you, so it's an ordinary stateful messaging service. Two rules are WebRTC's own: buffer candidates that land before their description, and let one peer yield when both offer at once.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:① connect with a token② join, get the room snapshot③ offer relayed④ answer relayed⑤ candidates trickle both ways⑥ early ones buffered until the description lands⑦ media up, channel kept for renegotiation

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does JSEP specify about signaling transport? Nothing: "left entirely up to the application" (RFC 9429 §3.1).
The three protocol messages? Offer, answer, ICE candidate. Everything else is your app.
Why buffer candidates? addIceCandidate fails before setRemoteDescription completes.
Glare, and the fix? Both offer at once; the polite peer rolls back and accepts.
Signaling down: what still works? Live calls. New calls and renegotiation fail.
Draw by hand: signaling with shared room state Caller, signaling node, room store, callee; offer and answer through the store's channel; candidates both ways.

The idea

In staging, both browsers land on the same signaling node and every call connects. In production there are four nodes behind a load balancer. The caller sits on node 1 and the callee on node 2, and the offer goes nowhere because node 1 has never heard of the callee. You add sticky sessions, and a deploy now breaks calls mid-negotiation. Then calls that do route still fail one time in ten: a candidate arrived while the offer was being applied, and the browser rejected it.

None of that is WebRTC. JSEP gives you a state machine for creating and applying descriptions and is "totally decoupled" from how they travel. So signaling is a messaging service you design: room membership in a shared store, a channel per room that any node can publish to, a token checked at connect, and two WebRTC-specific rules in the client.

The trade: you get to choose any transport, and you pay with a stateful, authenticated service you operate, whose failures stop calls from starting.

How it works

One call between peers on different nodes. Neither node holds the room; the store does.

The store's channel replaces instance affinity, so either node can restart and its clients reconnect anywhere.

Rule What actually happens
The message set Offer, answer and candidates have ordering rules. Presence, mute state and chat are your app; keep them separate.
Ordering Handlers are async. One ordered socket still lets a candidate run before setRemoteDescription finishes, so queue and flush.
Glare Both peers fire negotiationneeded. The polite peer rolls back and answers; the impolite one ignores the incoming offer. Both run the same code.
Lifetime It goes idle, not away. Screen share, a new track and an ICE restart after a network change are fresh offers.
The middle The LB's idle timer cuts silent sockets, and the store's channel carries every peer message. Heartbeats and a shared channel are mandatory.

Evolution

Lineage:2002 offer/answer (RFC 3264)2021 JSEP (RFC 8829) and Trickle ICE (RFC 8838)2024 JSEP revised (RFC 9429)2025 WHIP (RFC 9725)
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026, for the model; 🔵 for WHIP, a 2025 RFC that standardises signaling as one HTTP POST for ingest.
  • Changed in the W3C API: setLocalDescription() with no argument creates the offer or answer itself. Perfect negotiation relies on that to make both peers' code identical.
  • What's next and what won't change: HTTP-shaped signaling is spreading for one-known-peer cases (WHIP for ingest, WHEP still a draft, provider APIs). For rooms between users, it stays a service you write.

On the wire

Illustrative client: the two rules that cause most signaling bugs, after MDN's perfect negotiation pattern.

const polite = myId > peerId;                   // any rule both sides agree on
let makingOffer = false; const early = [];      // candidates that beat their description
pc.onnegotiationneeded = async () => {
  makingOffer = true;
  await pc.setLocalDescription();               // creates the offer implicitly
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ description: pc.localDescription }));
  makingOffer = false;
};
ws.onmessage = async ({ data }) => {
  const { description, candidate } = JSON.parse(data);
  if (description) {
    const collision = description.type === "offer" && (makingOffer || pc.signalingState !== "stable");
    if (collision && !polite) return;           // impolite peer ignores the incoming offer
    await pc.setRemoteDescription(description); // polite peer: implicit rollback
    while (early.length) await pc.addIceCandidate(early.shift());
    if (description.type === "offer") { await pc.setLocalDescription(); ws.send(JSON.stringify({ description: pc.localDescription })); }
  } else if (pc.remoteDescription) await pc.addIceCandidate(candidate);
  else early.push(candidate);                   // the queue that fixes the race
};

Break it: if messages arrive in order on one WebSocket, can a candidate beat the offer?

# a model of the browser: set_remote is async (5 ms), each message fires its own handler
async def on_message(m):
    if m == "offer": await pc.set_remote(m); flush(pending)
    elif buffered and pc.remote is None: pending.append(m)
    else: await pc.add_candidate(m)        # raises if no remote description yet
await asyncio.gather(*(on_message(m) for m in ["offer", "cand0", "cand1", "cand2", "cand3"]))
# look for: candidates rejected even though "offer" was delivered first
# naive belief predicts: zero rejections, because the socket is ordered

Run on Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026. It's a model of the event loop, not a browser. The naive handler rejected 4 of 4 candidates and the buffered one rejected none. Delivery order isn't processing order once a handler awaits.

Measure it

  • See it: log each signaling message with signalingState on both peers; correct is stable → have-local-offer → stable on one side, with no addIceCandidate errors on the other.
  • In production: time to connected per session, split into signaling, ICE and DTLS; addIceCandidate failures per session; signaling reconnects per client per hour. A rising reconnect rate is the early sign of an idle timer.
  • Bounded by: a deploy's reconnect storm → shared room state plus jittered reconnects. A negotiation that never settles → a client setup timeout, rollback, then one retry.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Signaling is the channel that carries the offer, the answer and the ICE candidates before two peers can talk, and WebRTC deliberately doesn't define it. It's a stateful messaging service you build, usually on WebSockets: room state in a shared store, a channel per room, auth at connect. Clients need two rules: buffer early candidates, and run perfect negotiation for glare. Once media flows it goes idle, but it stays up for renegotiation.

Q · Mechanism — Why did the spec leave signaling out, and what crosses it? Decoupling: SIP, XMPP and proprietary systems already existed, and mandating one would have locked WebRTC out of the rest. So JSEP defines only the state machine; the bytes are text any channel can carry. Three things cross: the SDP offer, the answer and candidates. The SDP holds the DTLS fingerprint, so signaling integrity is media security. Authenticate the channel, and don't treat it as a dumb pipe.

Q · Trade-off — WebSocket, server-sent events, or one HTTP POST? It follows from how peers find each other. Between users who don't know each other, the server must push an incoming call, so a WebSocket is the default, and you pay its operational bill. When the far end is one known service, a single POST carrying the offer and returning the answer is the whole design. WHIP standardises that for ingest, and model providers use it for realtime voice. No rooms, no push, so no socket tier.

Q · Failure — Calls fail to start, calls in progress are fine, every dashboard is green. What ran out? Usually nothing visible: an idle timer. A signaling socket carries nothing between calls, so a proxy or LB closes it, the client still shows online, and the incoming offer is never delivered. The other candidates are connection slots or file descriptors on the tier, because idle clients far outnumber active calls. Confirm with reconnects per client and connections per node against their limit. Fix with heartbeats under the shortest idle timer, and size the tier by connections, not calls.

Q · Design — Signaling for rooms, reconnects, and an agent that can be invited. The binding constraint is that the tier holding room state is the one you restart most. So nodes are stateless front ends, membership lives in a store, and peers reach each other through per-room channels, not affinity. A client reconnects to any node and gets a snapshot. The message set stays small: join, leave, offer, answer, candidate, snapshot. The agent joins as an ordinary participant with its own token. Watch time to connected split by phase. See the WebRTC flow design.

Compare

Signaling transport Server push What breaks When you'd pick it
WebSocket yes idle timers, deploy storms, cross-node routing rooms between users, the default
SSE plus POST server to client only one held response per client push-only needs, HTTP auth and logs for free
One HTTP POST (WHIP, provider APIs) none can't deliver an incoming call one known peer, no room state
SIP yes complexity and scarce skills telephony interop only

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Transport JSEP specifies none addressing, retransmission, forking, glare are the app's spec: RFC 9429 §3.1
Server legs before checks can start 4 offer in and out, answer in and out; candidates overlap derived: two relayed messages
signalingState values 6 stable, two offer states, two pranswer states, closed spec: W3C WebRTC
WHIP exchange 1 POST, 201 Created with the answer later candidates via PATCH spec: RFC 9725 §4
Candidates rejected, naive vs buffered 4 of 4 vs 0 of 4 async model, 5 ms apply time measured: Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Signaling is part of WebRTC; I just haven't found the API"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: everything else in the stack has a browser API.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: JSEP is "totally decoupled" from how descriptions travel, including addressing, retransmission, forking and glare.
    ↳ Think instead: there's no API because there's no spec. Design it like any messaging service.
  • "Signaling is done once the call connects"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: media flows peer to peer and the socket goes quiet.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: screen share, a new track and an ICE restart after a Wi-Fi to cellular switch are fresh offers. A closed socket can't recover any of them.
    ↳ Think instead: idle is not finished. Keep the channel and its heartbeat for the life of the call.
  • "One ordered WebSocket means candidates can't beat the offer"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: TCP delivers in order, so the offer is handled first.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the offer's handler awaits setRemoteDescription, and the next message's handler runs meanwhile. The run above rejected 4 of 4.
    ↳ Think instead: delivery order isn't processing order. Queue candidates until the description is applied.
  • Not the same: JSEP vs signaling
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "how the offer and answer happen".
    ↳ Difference: JSEP is the state machine inside the browser; signaling is the channel you run between browsers.
    ↳ Think instead: JSEP owns establishment, your app owns transport. Bugs in ordering and glare live at the seam.
  • Don't build a WebSocket tier for one known peer.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every tutorial starts with a signaling server.
    ↳ What goes wrong: rooms, presence and reconnect logic for a far end that never changes.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: one HTTP POST carrying the offer and returning the answer, as WHIP and provider APIs do.
  • Don't route peers by instance affinity.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: sticky sessions make two peers meet on one node in staging.
    ↳ What goes wrong: every deploy and scale event breaks negotiations in flight, and peers on different nodes never meet.
    ↳ Do instead: shared room state and a per-room channel; nodes stay interchangeable.
  • Shelf life: the model and the two client rules are durable. Which cases get a standard HTTP signaling (WHIP done, WHEP in draft) is still moving.

Connections

Path:the three APIssignalingSDPICE, STUN, TURN
  • Builds on WebSocket: the usual transport underneath.
  • Owned elsewhere: SDP owns what the messages contain; ICE owns where candidates come from.
  • Contrasts with sticky sessions: the affinity that shared room state replaces.
  • Bounded by WebSocket operations: heartbeats, drains and jittered reconnects bound the tier's failures.
  • Decided in the WebRTC flow design: where signaling sits in the system.
  • Drilled in WebRTC call setup.

notes.title: SDP Offer/Answer — The Answer Is the Session
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 3264 §6: generating the answer · 📜 RFC 9429 §5: JSEP SDP interaction · 📜 RFC 8866: SDP · WebRTC for the Curious: signaling

TL;DR

The offer lists everything the offerer can do: a media section per track, codecs, ICE credentials, the DTLS fingerprint and role. The answer returns the same sections narrowed to what the answerer accepts, and that answer is the session: nothing is counter-offered. The fingerprint rides in this text, so whoever can rewrite signaling can sit in the media path.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:createOfferoffer: Opus + G.722, actpass, fingerprintanswerer intersectsanswer: Opus only, activeboth stableDTLS client is the answerer

Recall

Prompt Answer
What is an answer, exactly? The offer's sections, narrowed to what the answerer accepts. It's binding.
How is a media section rejected? Port set to zero; the section stays in place (RFC 3264 §6).
Which line makes signaling security-critical? a=fingerprint: the DTLS certificate hash the media must match.

The idea

Both browsers support H.264, the negotiation succeeds, and there's no video. Reading the answer shows why: the answerer put port 0 on the video section, so it was rejected, and anything absent from the answer isn't in the session. There was no failed negotiation to catch, because offer/answer isn't a negotiation between equals.

An offer is a declaration of capability, a superset. The answer picks from it, and the pick is final until somebody sends a new offer. Every later change, from screen share to an ICE restart, goes through the same machinery with a fresh offer.

The trade: two messages settle a whole session, and you pay with a terse text format whose small edits break media without breaking negotiation.

How it works

One exchange. Each side's signalingState leaves stable and comes back.

The actpass-to-active step decides who opens DTLS: JSEP says answerers SHOULD take active (RFC 9429 §5.3.1).

Rule What actually happens
Sections One m= per media section. The answer has exactly as many, in the same order, so the k-th answers the k-th.
Rejection Port 0 on a section rejects it. Removing it would shift the meaning of every section after it.
Direction sendrecv, sendonly, recvonly, inactive, per section and per side. A listen-only agent answers recvonly on the user's audio.
Identity a=fingerprint pins the DTLS certificate and a=ice-ufrag / a=ice-pwd authenticate the checks.
The middle A gateway or SIP device may reject what browsers emit, which is the honest reason people edit SDP.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. RFC 3264 (2002) still defines the model; RFC 8866 (2021) replaced RFC 4566 as the SDP grammar.
  • Changed in RFC 9429: the max-bundle policy is deprecated in favour of an identical must-bundle, because implementations had assumed BUNDLE was already negotiated.
  • What's next and what won't change: APIs keep replacing string edits (setCodecPreferences, setParameters). The answer-is-binding model won't change.

On the wire

An illustrative offer excerpt, one audio section, with the lines that decide the session.

v=0
o=- 4611731400430051336 2 IN IP4 127.0.0.1
a=group:BUNDLE 0                       ← all sections share one transport
m=audio 9 UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF 111 9      ← payload types offered, in preference order
a=mid:0
a=ice-ufrag:EsAw                       ← authenticates ICE checks for this session
a=ice-pwd:bP+XJMM09aR8AiX1jdukzR6Y
a=fingerprint:sha-256 0F:74:31:25:…    ← the DTLS certificate the far side must present
a=setup:actpass                        ← "you choose": the answer says active or passive
a=sendrecv
a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2              ← Opus is always declared as 48 kHz, 2 channels
a=fmtp:111 minptime=10;useinbandfec=1  ← in-band FEC on
a=rtpmap:9 G722/8000

The answer would keep m=audio, drop payload type 9, and set a=setup:active.

Measure it

  • See it: log pc.localDescription.sdp and pc.remoteDescription.sdp on both sides; correct is the same number of m= lines, no zero ports you didn't intend, and matching codecs.
  • In production: per session, negotiated codec and rejected sections from getStats(), plus calls that reach connected with zero inbound bytes. That pattern means a section or codec was lost in negotiation.
  • Bounded by: a rewritten fingerprint → authenticated, encrypted signaling. A munging edit that breaks on a browser update → a test that fails when the munge stops being needed.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: SDP is the text the peers exchange to agree on a session. The offer lists media sections, codecs with payload types, ICE credentials, the DTLS fingerprint and actpass. The answer returns the same sections narrowed to what it accepts, and that answer is the session. Four things matter when debugging: m= sections, a=rtpmap, a=fingerprint and direction. Prefer APIs to editing the string.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a rewritten SDP line compromise the media? DTLS authenticates whatever certificate a=fingerprint names, and that line arrives over signaling, not over DTLS. An attacker who can rewrite signaling swaps in their own fingerprint, terminates DTLS on both sides and relays the media decrypted. Nothing in the media plane notices. So signaling integrity is media security, and the signaling channel needs authentication and TLS.

Q · Trade-off — How much should an application touch the SDP? As little as possible. setCodecPreferences orders codecs, RTCRtpSender.setParameters sets bitrate and encodings, and transceiver direction controls sending. They survive browser updates. Editing the string ("munging") lasts because a few things still have no API, mostly interop with SIP equipment. It's brittle: payload numbers are per session and section order matters, so an edit that works today can produce a connected call with no media after the next release.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
m= lines in an answer exactly as many as the offer the k-th answers the k-th spec: RFC 3264 §6
Rejected section port 0 the section stays in place spec: RFC 3264 §6
DTLS role in an offer actpass answer: active or passive, SHOULD be active spec: RFC 9429 §5.2.1, §5.3.1

Pitfalls

  • "Offer and answer negotiate, both sides give a bit"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the word "negotiation" suggests rounds.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the offer proposes and the answer selects, once. Anything it omits is gone until a new offer.
    ↳ Think instead: the answer is the session. Read it first when media is missing.
  • "Tampering with SDP is a privacy issue at most"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it looks like a description, not a credential.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a=fingerprint is the only link between signaling identity and the DTLS certificate encrypting the media.
    ↳ Think instead: SDP integrity is media security.
  • Not the same: a rejected section vs a removed one
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both mean "no video".
    ↳ Difference: rejection sets port 0 and keeps the slot; removal breaks the k-th to k-th pairing.
    ↳ Think instead: sections are positional. Never delete one; reject it.
  • Don't parse SDP with regexes to learn session state.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the codec and candidates are right there in the text.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the format shifts between browser releases, and the parser breaks silently.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: read getStats() and the transceiver APIs, which are stable.
  • Don't munge SDP as routine configuration.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one string edit fixes today's problem.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a later release reorders or renumbers, and calls connect with no media.
    ↳ Do instead: use the APIs; keep a munge only for a named gateway, with a test and an owner.
  • Shelf life: RFC 3264's model is durable. Which edits still need munging shrinks with each browser release.

Connections

Path:signalingSDPICE, STUN, TURN
  • Carried by signaling, whose integrity this note makes a security requirement.
  • Feeds ICE: a=ice-ufrag and a=ice-pwd authenticate its checks.
  • Owned elsewhere: the transport stack card owns DTLS-SRTP; audio for engineers owns codecs.
  • Builds on the three APIs: createOffer and setLocalDescription produce this text.

notes.title: ICE, STUN & TURN — Finding a Path Through NAT, and Paying for the Relay
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 8445 §5.1.2: ICE candidate priority · 📜 RFC 8489: STUN · 📜 RFC 8656 §3: TURN overview · WebRTC for the Curious: connecting

TL;DR

ICE gathers every address where you might be reachable, pairs them with the far side's, probes the pairs in priority order with STUN checks, and keeps the best one that works in both directions. STUN is one stateless question, "what address do you see me from?". TURN is a relay that carries every packet of the call. Relay share is your bill and your latency floor, and your users' networks set it, not your code.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:① host candidate② STUN Binding: "you appear as 203.0.113.9:51820"③ TURN Allocate, 600 s lifetime④ trickle to the peer⑤ checks in priority order⑥ peer-reflexive learned from an inbound check⑦ controlling agent nominates

Recall

Prompt Answer
The four candidate types? Host, server-reflexive, peer-reflexive, relayed.
Recommended type preferences? 126 host, 110 peer-reflexive, 100 server-reflexive, 0 relayed.
What does a STUN Binding response carry? The source address and port the server saw, XORed with the magic cookie.
Can a relay outrank a reflexive candidate? Never: type preference is multiplied by 2²⁴.
TURN allocation and permission lifetimes? 600 s and 300 s unless refreshed (RFC 8656 §3.2, §3.3).
Draw by hand: gather, check, nominate A asks STUN and TURN; candidates trickle; checks fail on host, succeed on reflexive; nominate.

The idea

A user at home calls a colleague in an office. The home router reuses one external port for every destination; the office firewall picks a new port for each destination. With only a STUN server configured, the call sits in checking for seconds and then goes to failed. Every pair you advertised points at a port the office NAT will never use toward you.

ICE doesn't try to predict any of that. Both sides offer everything: the local address, the address STUN saw, and an address on a TURN relay. Both probe every pair at once, because each outbound probe opens the mapping that admits the other side's. The priority order guarantees the relay is used only when nothing better worked. Here, the relay pair is the one that succeeds, and the call connects.

What it costs depends on which pair won. A direct pair costs one STUN round trip during setup and nothing after. A relayed pair sends every packet of the call through your server, both ways, for the whole call.

The trade: ICE connects nearly everyone, and you pay with a relay fleet whose load is set by your users' firewalls.

How it works

Gathering, then checks. The two-way check is what makes a pair valid, because NAT filtering is directional.

STUN costs one round trip per server during gathering. TURN costs an allocation now and a relay leg for every packet later, but only if its pair wins.

Priority is arithmetic, and the type term swamps everything else (RFC 8445 §5.1.2.1, component 1):

priority = 2^24·type + 2^8·local + (256 − component)
best relay   = 2^24·0   + 2^8·65535 + 255 = 16,777,215
worst srflx  = 2^24·100 + 2^8·0     + 255 = 1,677,721,855   ← 100× the best relay
pair priority = 2^32·min(G,D) + 2·max(G,D) + (G>D ? 1 : 0)   ← same order on both sides
Rule What actually happens
Valid pair A check and its response must succeed, and the response's source must equal the request's target (RFC 8445 §7.2.5.2.1).
Peer-reflexive A check from an address nobody advertised becomes a new candidate. It rescues pairs when one NAT reuses its mapping.
Nomination The controlling agent flags one valid pair. Media can flow on any valid pair before that.
STUN vs TURN STUN answers and forgets. TURN holds an allocation, permissions and timers, and forwards every packet.
The middle NAT mapping and filtering decide which pairs can work; NAT types has the matrix.

Evolution

Lineage:2008 STUN (RFC 5389)2010 ICE (RFC 5245) and TURN (RFC 5766)2018 ICE revised (RFC 8445)2020 STUN (RFC 8489) and TURN (RFC 8656) revised
  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. Every WebRTC stack implements it, and relay placement is an operational practice: Cloudflare, for one, runs TURN on anycast.
  • Changed in RFC 8445: data may flow on any valid pair before nomination, so "aggressive nomination" has no purpose any more. Agents signal the new behaviour with the ice2 option.
  • What's next and what won't change: IPv6 removes NAT for peers that both have it, and SFUs with public addresses shrink the hard cases. Some networks will always block UDP, so a relay over TLS on 443 stays.

On the wire

A STUN Binding exchange, captured from our own 20-line server on 127.0.0.1 with Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026. The decoded answer is the client's own source address, because that's all STUN reports.

request  : 00 01 00 00 21 12 a4 42 + 12-byte transaction id
           │     │     └ magic cookie 0x2112A442 (RFC 8489 §5)
           │     └ length 0: no attributes
           └ Binding request
response : 01 01 00 0c 21 12 a4 42 … 00 20 00 08 00 01 f8 1d 5e 12 a4 43
           └ Binding success      └ XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS, IPv4, port and address XORed
decoded  : 127.0.0.1:55567   my socket: 127.0.0.1:55567   same transaction id: True

The XOR exists so a NAT that rewrites addresses it finds in payloads can't corrupt the one field the protocol is for.

Break it: can a relay that answers first beat a slower reflexive pair?

pri = lambda typ, local: 2**24 * typ + 2**8 * local + (256 - 1)   # RFC 8445 §5.1.2.1
print(pri(0, 65535))    # best possible relay        → 16777215
print(pri(100, 0))      # worst possible srflx       → 1677721855
print(pri(126, 65535))  # best possible host         → 2130706431
# look for: every srflx priority above every relay priority
# naive belief predicts: some local preference lets a fast relay win

Run on Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026. The worst reflexive candidate is 100 times the best relay, so answer time never enters the order. A relay wins only when no better pair is valid, and forcing it in a test needs iceTransportPolicy: "relay".

Measure it

  • See it: chrome://webrtc-internals, or getStats(): the nominated candidate-pair and its local candidate's candidateType. Then force iceTransportPolicy: "relay"; correct is a connected call whose local type is relay.
  • In production: relay share per session, split by region and customer network; time to connected p99; egress per TURN node. A step in relay share with no deploy means a customer's firewall changed.
  • Bounded by: relay saturation → per-node capacity alarms and edge relays. An abused relay → short-lived per-session credentials and allocation quotas. A hung check list → ICE timeout and one ICE restart.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: ICE finds a working path between two endpoints behind NAT. Each side gathers a local address, the address a STUN server saw, and a relayed address on TURN. Both probe every pair with STUN checks and nominate the best that works both ways. STUN is a free, stateless question. TURN relays the whole call, so relay share drives your bandwidth bill and latency floor. Users' firewalls set it.

Q · Mechanism — Why must a check succeed in both directions? NAT filtering is directional. A's outbound check creates the mapping that admits B's packets, and B's check does the same for A, so a pair proven one way may still be dropped the other way. ICE also demands symmetry: the response must come from the exact address the request went to, or the pair fails. Peer-reflexive candidates come from this step, when a check arrives from an address nobody advertised.

Q · Trade-off — STUN is nearly free and TURN isn't. What do you deploy? Both, sized differently. STUN is one request and response with no state, so a small pool anywhere public is enough. TURN carries relayed sessions × bitrate, in and out, with an allocation per client refreshed every 600 s. Add TURN over TLS on 443 for networks that block UDP. It puts TCP under the media, which is worse, and still better than no call. Relay share varies too much by population to quote, so measure yours.

Q · Failure — After a big enterprise customer lands, audio degrades for some users, and every connectivity metric is green. What ran out? TURN bandwidth. Every relayed session pushes full media through the node both ways, so a NIC or the egress budget saturates long before CPU. Each client's bandwidth estimator lowers bitrate, so it reads as poor quality, not failure. Confirm by splitting quality by candidate type: the bad sessions are the relayed ones, on the hot nodes. Fix with capacity at the edge near those users and quotas per allocation.

Q · Design — Where do STUN and TURN go for a global product with an SFU? The binding constraint is that a relay is a detour on every packet. So relays sit at the edge near users, not beside a central media tier, and anycast reaches the nearest without client logic. STUN placement barely matters: one round trip once. An SFU with a public address shrinks TURN's job, because one side of every pair is reachable. Relay then serves mostly UDP-blocked networks, over TLS on 443. Watch relay share by network first. See egress cost and the WebRTC flow design.

Compare

STUN TURN over UDP TURN over TLS on 443 When you'd pick it
Traffic through it one request and response the whole call, both ways the whole call, over TCP STUN always; TURN for real users
State held none allocation, permissions, channels the same, plus a TLS session TURN needs a capacity plan
Latency added one RTT, during gathering a detour on every packet a detour plus head-of-line stalls place relays near users
Candidate type server-reflexive, 100 relayed, 0 relayed, 0 ICE uses relays last

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Type preferences 126 / 110 / 100 / 0 host, prflx, srflx, relay spec: RFC 8445 §5.1.2.2
Best relay vs worst srflx priority 16,777,215 vs 1,677,721,855 component 1 derived: RFC 8445 §5.1.2.1
Check pacing Ta 50 ms default one new check per tick spec: RFC 8445 §14.2
STUN and TURN ports 3478 TCP and UDP; 5349 for TLS and DTLS turns: on 443 is a deployment choice spec: RFC 8489 §8.1
TURN allocation 600 s default, refresh to keep; max ≤ 3,600 s recommended per client spec: RFC 8656 §3.2, §7.2
TURN permission 300 s unless refreshed per peer address spec: RFC 8656 §3.3
Relay share measure it varies with your user population no universal figure

Pitfalls

  • "STUN punches a hole through the NAT"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the step that happens before traversal works.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: STUN only reports the address it saw. Your own outbound check opens the mapping, and NAT behaviour decides whether the peer can use it.
    ↳ Think instead: STUN observes, checks punch. A per-destination NAT makes the observation useless.
  • "TURN is a fallback, so it needs no capacity plan"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: its candidates have the lowest priority.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: every session that lands on it sends full media through it for the whole call, both ways.
    ↳ Think instead: last in priority, first on the bill. Plan bandwidth and egress per relayed session.
  • "ICE picks the fastest path"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it probes everything, so it must pick the quickest.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it picks the highest-priority valid pair, and type dominates; the run above shows any reflexive pair beating any relay.
    ↳ Think instead: priority, not speed. Path quality isn't in the formula.
  • Not the same: STUN vs TURN
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: same port, same message format, often the same server.
    ↳ Difference: STUN is stateless and answers once; TURN holds allocations and carries every packet.
    ↳ Think instead: size STUN by requests and TURN by megabits.
  • Don't ship static TURN credentials.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one username in the client config just works.
    ↳ What goes wrong: anyone can pull it from your JavaScript and relay their own traffic on your bill.
    ↳ Do instead: short-lived credentials issued per session by your backend, plus quotas per allocation.
  • Don't build a relay fleet before you know your relay share.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: TURN sounds like core infrastructure from day one.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you size and operate edge relays for a load you've only guessed.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: start on a managed TURN service, measure relay share by network, then build where egress cost justifies it.
  • Shelf life: the priority formula and lifetimes are durable. Managed TURN offerings and their prices change; check the current ones.

Connections

Path:signalingICE, STUN, TURNNAT typestopologies
  • Builds on NAT: mappings, and why an unsolicited packet has nothing to match.
  • Owned elsewhere: NAT types owns mapping and filtering; what WebRTC is for owns consent freshness.
  • Composes with anycast: one address that reaches the nearest relay.
  • Bounded by egress cost: where relay bandwidth becomes money.
  • Decided in the WebRTC flow design: where relays sit.
  • Drilled in TURN cost.

notes.title: NAT Types & Why P2P Fails — Mapping, Filtering, Hairpinning
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 4787: NAT behaviour for UDP · 📜 RFC 8445 §7.2.5: check outcomes · 📜 RFC 6598: shared address space · WebRTC for the Curious: connecting

TL;DR

Whether two peers connect directly depends on two independent NAT behaviours: mapping (does the NAT reuse one external port for every destination?) and filtering (who may send back through it?). A port that changes per destination makes the STUN-reported address useless to the peer, and if the other side filters by exact port, no direct pair exists. Only a relay works.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:A asks STUNNAT shows one mappingcandidates swappedboth send at onceeach send opens a mapping for the othera per-destination NAT picks a new portrelay

Recall

Prompt Answer
The two axes? Mapping (which external port) and filtering (who may reply).
"Symmetric NAT" in RFC 4787 terms? Address-and-port-dependent mapping: a new port per destination.
Hairpinning? Two hosts behind one NAT reaching each other via its public address. RFC 4787 requires it.

The idea

Two users on the same mobile carrier try a direct call, and it fails every time. Both sit behind carrier-grade NAT in 100.64.0.0/10, which hands out a fresh external port for each destination. The address the STUN server reported belonged to the conversation with the STUN server. When the peer aims at it, nothing on the carrier's side is waiting there.

"Symmetric NAT breaks P2P" is both too broad and too narrow: a per-destination NAT can work against a lenient peer, and a stable-port router that filters by exact port fails against it. RFC 4787's two axes explain both.

The trade: knowing the axes predicts which users will need a relay, but you can't change them, because they belong to networks you don't run.

How it works

A has a stable mapping. B's NAT picks a new port per destination, so its STUN port is useless to A.

The same per-destination NAT works against a lenient filter and fails against a strict one.

Rule What actually happens
Mapping Endpoint-independent reuses one port for all destinations. RFC 4787 REQ-1 says a NAT MUST behave this way; plenty of deployed ones don't.
Filtering Endpoint-independent admits anyone, address-dependent admits hosts you've sent to, address-and-port-dependent admits only the exact ports.
Hairpinning Two hosts behind one NAT reach each other via its public address. REQ-9 requires it; without it, ICE needs their host candidates.
The middle Carrier NAT in 100.64.0.0/10 (RFC 6598) puts many subscribers behind one address, with its own port policy.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. RFC 4787 (2007), updated by RFC 7857 (2016), is still the vocabulary.
  • Changed in RFC 4787 and RFC 5389: "full cone, restricted cone, port-restricted, symmetric" gave way to two axes. RFC 5389 dropped classic STUN's NAT-type detection because "many NATs did not fit cleanly into the types".
  • What's next and what won't change: IPv6 on both ends removes the problem. While NAT exists, probing beats classifying.

On the wire

Break it: is "at least one side has a stable port" enough for a direct path?

# model: both peers' NATs over all 3 mappings × 3 filterings; ICE-style simultaneous checks,
# peer-reflexive learning, and RFC 8445's rule that a response must come from where the check went
def direct(a, b): ...                     # True if any check gets a symmetric response back
fails = [(x, y) for x, y in pairings if not direct(x, y)]
# look for: pairings with a stable-port side that still need a relay
# naive belief predicts: none, because one cooperative side is enough

Run on Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026, as a model that ignores port prediction and timers. 22 of 45 pairings needed a relay.

Your NAT (mapping + filtering) Direct path against…
Stable port, filters by address or not at all every peer in the model
Stable port, filters by address and port only peers with a stable port
Port per destination, any filtering lenient peers; never another per-destination NAT

A stable port on one side isn't enough: the classic failure is port-restricted against symmetric.

Measure it

  • See it: query two different STUN servers from one socket; correct for an endpoint-independent NAT is the same reported port both times. Different ports mean a per-destination mapping.
  • In production: nominated candidate type per session (host, srflx, prflx, relay) grouped by network or carrier. A carrier whose sessions are mostly relayed is behind a per-destination NAT.
  • Bounded by: no direct pair → TURN catches the session; UDP blocked → TURN over TLS on 443. Relays bound the harm; nothing fixes the NAT.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Direct connection depends on two NAT behaviours. Mapping decides which external port the NAT uses: endpoint-independent reuses one, so the STUN-reported address works for the peer; address-and-port-dependent, the "symmetric" one, picks a new port per destination. Filtering decides who may reply. When a per-destination mapping meets strict filtering or another per-destination mapping, no pair works, and TURN is the only path.

Q · Mechanism — Why does hole punching work at all, and what breaks it? Outbound traffic creates mappings. When both send at once, each packet opens the door for the other's, so neither NAT forwards anything unsolicited; ICE's two-way checks are that send. It breaks on either axis: a per-destination mapping leaves the peer aiming at a stale port, and strict filtering drops a reply from a port you never sent to.

Q · Trade-off — How much effort should go into avoiding the relay? Not much at the client: the deciding behaviour is someone else's router, and only IPv6 candidates help much. The big lever is topological: an SFU with a public address turns every pair into client-to-server, where only one side is behind NAT. What still relays is mostly UDP-blocked networks, and for them TURN over TLS on 443 is the answer.

Compare

Mapping (RFC 4787) Older name Is the STUN address usable by a peer?
Endpoint-independent full, restricted or port-restricted cone yes: one port for every destination
Address-dependent none in the old scheme toward that peer's address only
Address-and-port-dependent symmetric no: new port per destination and port

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Carrier NAT space 100.64.0.0/10 shared between subscribers spec: RFC 6598
Pairings needing a relay 22 of 45 all mapping × filtering pairs measured: model, Python 3.15.0, 22 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "Symmetric NAT on either end means P2P fails"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the one-line rule most write-ups give.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a per-destination NAT can work against a lenient filter, and a stable-port NAT with strict filtering can fail against it.
    ↳ Think instead: look at both axes on both sides; it's the pairing that fails, not one NAT.
  • "Hole punching tricks the NAT"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the name sounds like an exploit.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: both sides send outbound, and each send creates the mapping that admits the other's packets.
    ↳ Think instead: the NAT works as designed. That's why per-destination mappings fail cleanly, not intermittently.
  • Not the same: mapping vs filtering
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the old cone names fused them into one list.
    ↳ Difference: mapping picks the external port; filtering decides which inbound packets that port accepts.
    ↳ Think instead: mapping decides where the peer aims; filtering decides whether it's let in.
  • Don't detect the NAT type and branch on it.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: classify once, then pick the right path.
    ↳ What goes wrong: NATs don't fit clean types, which is why RFC 5389 dropped the detection.
    ↳ Do instead: let ICE probe every pair; use classification only for diagnosis.
  • Don't tune direct paths when a public endpoint ends the problem.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: peer-to-peer feels cheaper, so every failure looks fixable.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you optimise an outcome decided by someone else's router.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: put a server with a public address, an SFU, in the path.
  • Shelf life: the axes are durable. The share of users behind carrier NAT shifts with IPv6 rollout.

Connections

Path:ICE, STUN, TURNNAT typestopologies
  • Builds on NAT: tables, ports per destination and timers.
  • Used by ICE, which probes these behaviours instead of classifying them.
  • Owned elsewhere: private vs public IP owns the address ranges; ICE owns check rules.
  • Contrasts with topologies: a public endpoint in the path, the fix this note can't make.

notes.title: Topologies — Mesh vs SFU vs MCU, and When a Media Server Earns Its Place
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 7667 §3.7: selective forwarding middlebox · WebRTC for the Curious: applied WebRTC · mediasoup v3: design

TL;DR

Mesh sends every stream from every client to every other client, so each uplink carries n−1 copies. An SFU takes one upload per client and forwards the packets each receiver needs without decoding them. An MCU decodes, mixes and re-encodes one stream per receiver. The SFU moves the quadratic from the weakest uplink in the call to a server you can size, which is why nearly everything modern uses one.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:each client uploads onceSFU terminates SRTP per participantreads RTP headerspicks streams and a simulcast layer per receiverrewrites sequence numbersforwards n−1 streams down

Recall

Prompt Answer
Client uplink in a mesh of n? n−1 streams; n(n−1)/2 connections across the call.
What does an SFU skip that an MCU does? Decoding and re-encoding. It forwards packets.
SFU server egress per room? n(n−1) streams, the term that dominates its bill.

The idea

A 1:1 product adds group calls on the same code, and five-person calls fall apart. Each laptop encodes and uploads its video four times. The weakest uplink freezes for everyone else while its owner's screen looks fine, so the bug report comes from the wrong user.

An SFU changes who does the copying. Each client sends one stream, or a few qualities of it, and the server forwards what each receiver should get, paying in bandwidth, not CPU. An MCU goes further: it decodes everything and sends one composite, which helps very weak receivers and costs a transcode per room.

The trade: an SFU gives every client a constant uplink, and you pay with server egress that grows as n(n−1) and a stateful tier to place and drain.

How it works

One sender, three receivers. The SFU picks a different layer for each, and the agent is just another subscriber.

Without simulcast, the weakest receiver sets one quality for everyone: mesh's failure, relocated.

The arithmetic decides it, with b the bitrate of one stream:

mesh  per client: up (n−1)·b, down (n−1)·b       ← the weakest uplink caps the room
SFU   per client: up b, down (n−1)·b             ← uplink constant
SFU   server:     in n·b, out n(n−1)·b           ← egress is the bill
MCU   server:     in n·b, out n·b, plus decode and encode work per room
n = 10, b = 1 Mbit/s (illustrative): mesh 9 Mbit/s up per laptop; SFU 90 Mbit/s out
Rule What actually happens
Codecs An SFU never runs one, so one node carries far more participants than an MCU on the same hardware.
Layers With simulcast the sender's uplink is the sum of its layers; the SFU's choice is only as good as each receiver's bandwidth estimate.
Server consumers Recording, transcription and agents subscribe like participants; mixing for them runs beside the SFU, not as the room's topology.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟢 Established, Nov 2026. RFC 7667 (2015) named the SFU a "selective forwarding middlebox"; LiveKit, mediasoup and Janus all forward rather than mix.
  • Changed by insertable streams: end-to-end encryption through an SFU is possible by encrypting frames above SRTP (W3C Encoded Transform, a working draft as of 25 June 2026). The SFU then can't inspect content, only headers.
  • What's next and what won't change: scalable codecs (SVC) carry layers in one stream, and cascaded SFUs span regions. Forwarding without decoding stays.

On the wire

Illustrative sender config for simulcast: three encodings of one camera track. The SFU forwards one per receiver.

pc.addTransceiver(camera, {
  direction: "sendonly",
  sendEncodings: [
    { rid: "h", maxBitrate: 1_200_000 },                          // big tiles
    { rid: "m", maxBitrate: 400_000, scaleResolutionDownBy: 2 },
    { rid: "l", maxBitrate: 120_000, scaleResolutionDownBy: 4 },  // thumbnails, weak links
  ],
});

Measure it

  • See it: chrome://webrtc-internals on the sender shows three outbound-rtp entries, one per rid; on a receiver, inbound-rtp shows which layer arrives as the tile size changes.
  • In production: SFU egress per room and node, and the layer forwarded per subscriber. A room whose subscribers all sit on the low layer has a sender problem.
  • Bounded by: a very large room → forward only the active speakers. A hot node → room placement with affinity, then cascading to a second SFU.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Three ways to connect more than two people. Mesh connects everyone directly, so each client uploads n−1 copies; it collapses at a handful of people. An SFU takes one upload per client and forwards selected packets without decoding, so client uplink is constant and server egress is n(n−1). An MCU decodes and mixes into one stream, cheap on bandwidth and expensive on CPU. The SFU is the default.

Q · Mechanism — What does an SFU actually do to the packets? Very little. It terminates ICE, DTLS and SRTP with each participant, so it decrypts and re-encrypts at the packet level, but it never decodes media. It reads RTP headers, decides which streams and which simulcast layer each receiver gets, rewrites sequence numbers and timestamps, and forwards. Cost per stream is bandwidth, not codec CPU.

Q · Trade-off — When do you introduce a media server, and would you switch modes at three people? As soon as a server consumes the media (recording, transcription, an agent), or past two people with video. Switching from peer-to-peer at three is two products: two media paths, two recording stories, and a transition that fires as the call gets more important. With any group or agent feature, run the SFU for every call.

Compare

Mesh SFU MCU When you'd pick it
Client up / down n−1 / n−1 1 / n−1, selectable 1 / 1 composite SFU and MCU both fix the uplink
Server work none forwarding decode, mix, encode MCU only for very weak receivers
Server bandwidth none n in, n(n−1) out n in, n out MCU is cheapest on bandwidth, dearest on CPU
Encrypted to the far peer the SFU the MCU only mesh is end to end by default
Pick when two people, no server consumer anything else legacy interop, one fixed layout SFU is the default

Pitfalls

  • Not the same: SFU vs TURN
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both sit in the middle and forward media.
    ↳ Difference: TURN forwards opaque packets between two endpoints; an SFU terminates SRTP, reads headers and chooses streams and layers per receiver.
    ↳ Think instead: an SFU is a participant; TURN is a pipe. Only the SFU can adapt quality.
  • "Mesh is fine for small groups because there's no server bottleneck"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no server sounds like no limit.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the bottleneck moved to the weakest uplink, which you can't provision or see, and its failure shows on everyone else's screen.
    ↳ Think instead: no server means no capacity you control.
  • "Our SFU calls are end-to-end encrypted"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: WebRTC encrypts everything, so the claim seems free.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: SRTP ends at the SFU, which can see the media. End to end needs frame encryption above SRTP.
    ↳ Think instead: encrypted to the server by default; end to end is an extra layer that blinds the SFU.
  • Don't treat an SFU as a stateless web tier.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it sits behind a load balancer like everything else.
    ↳ What goes wrong: participants hold transport, keys and subscriptions on one node, so a restart drops rooms, and a room can't be split across nodes without cascading.
    ↳ Do instead: place rooms with affinity, drain before deploys, and plan cascading for big rooms.
  • Don't run a media server for 1:1 calls nothing on the server needs.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one uniform path sounds tidy.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you pay egress and run a tier for media that could have gone peer to peer.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: peer-to-peer with a TURN fallback, until recording, groups or an agent arrive.
  • Shelf life: the arithmetic is durable. Encoded Transform is still a working draft, and SVC support varies by codec and browser.

Connections

Path:NAT typestopologiesWebRTC vs WebSocketWebRTC for voice AI
  • Builds on ICE: an SFU's public address removes most traversal trouble.
  • Owned elsewhere: rooms, participants, tracks owns the room model; the media pipeline card owns simulcast and bandwidth estimation.
  • Used by WebRTC for voice AI: the agent subscribes like any participant.
  • Composes with sticky sessions: routing to a stateful media server.

notes.title: WebRTC for Voice AI — The Transport on Each Hop Between a Microphone and a Model
notes.html:
References

OpenAI: Realtime API with WebRTC · Cloudflare: TURN and anycast · 📜 RFC 8834: RTP in WebRTC

TL;DR

A voice agent's media goes browser → nearest edge over WebRTC → a worker running speech recognition, the model and speech synthesis → back as an ordinary audio track. Each hop's transport follows its loss: WebRTC over the last mile, whatever the provider recommends inside. Count the hops between the microphone and the model: after you choose the model, transport is the latency you can still buy back.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:① Opus over SRTP to the nearest edge② SFU forwards the track to a worker in the same region③ worker streams to the model provider④ synthesised audio published as a track⑤ SFU forwards it to the user⑥ worker stops playback

Recall

Prompt Answer
Why WebRTC from the browser? Loss concealment and congestion control on a lossy last mile.
Where does the agent sit? As a participant on the SFU, not on a special path.
How does a browser reach the provider without your API key? Your server exchanges its SDP offer, or mints a short-lived token.

The idea

A team ships its voice agent over a WebSocket from the browser to one server region, and users on another continent wait a long beat for every reply. The long haul crosses an ocean every turn, and on lossy mobile links TCP stalls each lost frame, as WebRTC vs WebSocket shows. Prompt work can't recover either.

The standard shape fixes both by placement. The browser talks WebRTC to an edge near the user, so loss is concealed on the only lossy hop. The worker sits beside that edge, and it opens the provider connection from the same region, so each turn's long haul happens once, on a clean server path. Barge-in and echo handling run on the same media path (barge-in, echo cancellation).

The trade: you remove transport time, and you pay with an edge, a worker pool and relays in every region you serve.

How it works

One turn, hop by hop: what each hop costs, with no measured timings.

Step Hop Transport Loss on the path What it costs per turn
1 browser → edge SFU WebRTC, SRTP over UDP high: Wi-Fi, cellular client-to-edge one-way delay, plus the jitter buffer
2 edge SFU → worker forwarded track, same region negligible a short in-region hop
3 worker → model provider the provider's server transport low the provider round trip, unavoidable
4 relayed session only TURN detour as step 1 the detour twice: inbound audio and the reply
5 worker → edge → browser published track, then WebRTC as step 1 the same edge path, in reverse

The relay row is the one placement decides:

detour   = (client→relay + relay→edge) − client→edge   ← one direction
per turn = 2 × detour                                   ← user audio in, agent audio out
fix      = relays near users, beside the edge          ← detour → 0
  • Signaling is your server, once: the browser's offer goes through your backend so the API key never reaches it. That puts one round trip to your server in session setup, not in every turn.
