  • The agent is a participant: it joins the room with its own token (tokens and dispatch), so recording, captions and handoffs reuse the SFU.

Evolution

  • Maturity today: 🟡 Maturing, Nov 2026. Model providers ship WebRTC endpoints, and their guidance is still moving: OpenAI now recommends WebRTC for its live voice model in browser, mobile and server applications.
  • Changed in provider APIs: besides minting a short-lived token for the browser, a provider may let your server exchange the browser's SDP directly. That's simpler, at the cost of your server sitting in session setup.
  • What's next and what won't change: speech-to-speech models remove hops inside the worker. The last mile stays lossy, so WebRTC at the edge stays.

On the wire

Illustrative backend, after OpenAI's unified interface as documented in Nov 2026: the browser posts its offer to you, and you forward it with the key the browser never sees.

app.post("/session", express.text({ type: "application/sdp" }), async (req, res) => {
  const fd = new FormData();
  fd.set("sdp", req.body);                    // the browser's SDP offer
  fd.set("session", JSON.stringify(config));  // model, voice, tools: decided server-side
  const r = await fetch("https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY}` }, // stays on the server
    body: fd,
  });
  res.type("application/sdp").send(await r.text()); // the SDP answer, back to the browser
});

Measure it

  • See it: timestamps per hop for one turn, from end of user speech to first agent audio, as measuring a turn defines; correct is every hop's share known, none guessed.
  • In production: relay share for voice sessions, edge-to-worker RTT per region, and turn latency p99 per user region. A region whose p99 is high with a normal model time has a placement or relay problem.
  • Bounded by: a slow provider → a per-turn timeout and the degradation ladder. A relay detour → regional TURN beside the edge.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A realtime voice agent is a latency budget with a model in the middle. The standard shape is browser to a nearby edge over WebRTC, an SFU forwarding to a worker that runs recognition, the model and synthesis, and the reply published back as an ordinary track. WebRTC sits at the edge because the last mile loses packets. The design question is which hops you can remove, because each one spends budget you can't recover.

Q · Mechanism — What does each hop carry, and why that transport? The last mile carries Opus over SRTP, because that's where loss is. The SFU forwards the track inside the region, a short clean hop. The worker talks to the provider over the server transport the provider recommends; as of Nov 2026, OpenAI's live voice model prefers WebRTC even there. The reply comes back as a published track, so it needs no new path.

Q · Trade-off — Browser straight to the provider's WebRTC endpoint, or through your own SFU and worker? Straight to the provider is the fewest hops and the least infrastructure: one session, your server only in setup. Your own SFU and worker earn their place when you need more than one model call can give: recording, a human joining, handoffs between agents, your own turn detection or tools on the hot path. Start direct; move to the SFU when a feature needs the media on your side (pipeline shapes).

Pitfalls

  • "The model's latency dominates, so transport hardly matters"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: model time is the biggest single number on the dashboard.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: after the model is chosen, its time is mostly fixed, while hops, relays and stalls are still yours to change.
    ↳ Think instead: transport is the budget you can still buy back. Measure it per hop.
  • Don't ship a provider API key to the browser.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the browser talks to the provider directly anyway.
    ↳ What goes wrong: anyone can lift the key from your JavaScript and bill to it.
    ↳ Do instead: exchange the SDP through your server, or mint a short-lived token per session.
  • Not the same: setup latency vs turn latency
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "how slow the agent feels".
    ↳ Difference: signaling and ICE are paid once per session; hops and relays are paid on every turn.
    ↳ Think instead: optimise per-turn hops first; a slower join is paid once.
  • Don't build an SFU and worker tier for a single-model demo.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the architecture production voice platforms show.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you run rooms, workers and relays to forward one stream to one model.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: browser to the provider's WebRTC endpoint, with your server exchanging the offer.
  • Don't optimise transport before measuring the split.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: hops are visible on a diagram.
    ↳ What goes wrong: if endpointing waits 700 ms for silence, a saved hop is noise.
    ↳ Do instead: time the turn by phase first, using the latency budget.
  • Shelf life: provider endpoints, session APIs and their transport advice change every few months; the hop arithmetic doesn't.

Connections

Path:topologiesWebRTC vs WebSocketWebRTC for voice AIvoice agents on the AI path
  • Owned elsewhere: the latency budget owns the turn's terms; rooms and tracks owns the room model.
  • Builds on topologies: the agent is a participant on the SFU.
  • Bounded by ICE, STUN, TURN: relay placement sets the detour.
  • Decided in scaling to 1,000 calls.
  • Drilled in WebRTC vs WebSocket channels.

notes.title: WebRTC vs WebSocket for Audio — What Happens to a Late Frame
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 8834: RTP in WebRTC · WebRTC for the Curious: media communication · MDN: getUserMedia()

TL;DR

Both move audio both ways in well under a second, so the choice isn't about capability. It's about loss: TCP won't deliver past a gap, so one lost segment makes every frame behind it late, and you hear a stall, then a burst. WebRTC conceals the lost frame and plays the rest on time, and it brings echo cancellation, a jitter buffer and congestion control. WebRTC where the last mile loses packets, WebSocket where it doesn't.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper packet
Flow:TCP: frame 3 lost4 and 5 held3 resent after ~1 RTT3, 4, 5 arrive together, late
UDP: frame 3 lostdecoder conceals it4 and 5 play on time

Recall

Prompt Answer
The one mechanism that decides it? TCP head-of-line blocking against UDP with concealment.
What do you build yourself over a WebSocket? Encoding, framing, a jitter buffer, loss handling, rate adaptation.
Frames late per loss in the model below? About 4 over TCP; 1 concealed over UDP.

The idea

Your voice prototype streams PCM over a WebSocket and sounds perfect on office Wi-Fi. On a train, the agent freezes for a beat, then rushes. TCP must deliver in order, so every frame behind a lost segment waits for its retransmission, and a 20 ms frame that arrives 100 ms late is worthless.

WebRTC inverts the priority. Over UDP a lost packet is just missing: the decoder fills that frame and everything after plays on time.

The trade: WebRTC keeps audio on time under loss, and you pay with ICE, TURN and a media server; a WebSocket is one connection, and you pay with a pipeline you write and stalls on bad networks.

How it works

The same lost frame on both transports.

The cost of one loss on TCP, with the model's inputs (20 ms frames, 60 ms RTT, a 40 ms playout buffer):

detect loss   = 3 later frames × 20 ms = 60 ms     ← fast retransmit waits for 3 duplicate ACKs
resend        = 1 RTT = 60 ms
stall         = 60 + 60 = 120 ms > 40 ms buffer    ← the buffer can't hide it
frames late   = (120 − 40) ÷ 20 = 4               ← the lost one plus the 3 queued behind it

TCP head-of-line blocking owns the general mechanism; the playout deadline is what makes it fatal for audio.

  • See it: run both transports through a link with a few percent loss; on WebRTC, getStats() shows concealedSamples rising while playback stays smooth.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Both carry audio both ways with low latency, so the choice is about loss. A WebSocket runs on TCP, which won't deliver past a gap, so one lost segment makes the frames behind it late. WebRTC runs on UDP and conceals a lost frame instead of waiting, and it brings echo cancellation, a jitter buffer and congestion control. On a clean network they're identical; on a phone with two bars, WebRTC.

Q · Mechanism — What happens to WebSocket audio when a packet drops? TCP retransmits, and the stack won't hand over bytes past the gap, so every queued frame waits one round trip plus detection. Those frames play late as a burst, or force a deeper buffer that never shrinks quickly. In the model, each loss cost about four late frames, against one concealed frame over UDP.

Q · Trade-off — When is a WebSocket the right call for audio? When the path barely loses packets: server to server in a region, wired internal tools, or a prototype. One connection, ordinary auth and logs, no ICE or TURN. In a browser the price is a pipeline you write: encoding, framing, a jitter buffer and reconnect. For a consumer mobile product, that's the wrong saving.

Pitfalls

  • "WebSocket is real-time, so it's fine for real-time audio"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's low latency, full duplex and already in the stack.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it's low latency when nothing is lost. Live media needs the transport to give up on late data, which TCP can't.
    ↳ Think instead: the question is what happens when a packet is lost, not the latency when none are.
  • "The difference is a few milliseconds either way"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: both transports benchmark the same on a clean path.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the gap is zero without loss and grows with it: about four late frames per lost packet in the model above.
    ↳ Think instead: compare distributions under loss, and decide on p99.
  • Not the same: WebRTC over UDP vs WebRTC relayed over TLS
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "the WebRTC path".
    ↳ Difference: TURN over TLS on 443 puts TCP under the media, so a relayed session stalls on loss like a WebSocket.
    ↳ Think instead: "we use WebRTC" isn't a guarantee for every session; check the nominated candidate type.
  • Don't benchmark this on office Wi-Fi.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the network you have.
    ↳ What goes wrong: without loss, the transports are indistinguishable, so the WebSocket prototype always passes.
    ↳ Do instead: test with a few percent loss and some jitter, or you've measured nothing about the choice.
  • Don't run WebRTC between your own services in one region.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: one transport end to end sounds consistent.
    ↳ What goes wrong: loss inside a data centre is negligible, so you take on ICE, DTLS and per-session state for no benefit.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: a WebSocket or gRPC stream for the hop, unless the provider says otherwise.
